particulars: All names, ages, dates, places, the agencies involved, physical measurements, probability figures, the sentence length and compensation amounts were dropped.

items.record: The text is a narrative summary of a wrongful rape conviction and exoneration that follows many actors over several years: "Josiah Sutton was convicted... and sentenced to 25 years in prison."
items.reading: A single official findings memo or closing determination, issued by one body with final authority, written in numbered findings and defined terms.
items.loss: This is the basic genre and subject of the case, and the reading gets it wrong.

items.record: The person on the margin is a Black teenager accused of rape, tried as an adult and imprisoned. What was at stake was his liberty: "certified to stand trial as an adult."
items.reading: A whistleblower, dissenting employee or complainant who depends on the institution for a job, licence or benefits.
items.loss: This is who the marginal party was and what they stood to lose, and the reading misidentifies both.

items.record: The accusation began with a street show-up identification based on hats, even though the description did not fit him: "about 6 inches taller and 60 pounds heavier than P.S.' description."
items.loss: This is how the error started: a mistaken eyewitness identification that ignored a clear physical mismatch.

items.record: The lab's DNA work was unreliable and its statistics were overstated. The jury heard "1 in 694,000", but a correct analysis gave "better than 1 chance in 8". The lab also produced two different profiles for the same victim.
items.reading: The record is honest on its surface and accurate in each part, and the institution does not need to lie.
items.loss: This is the central mechanism: forensic evidence that was flawed and misleadingly presented, which the reading wrongly treats as accurate.

items.record: Exculpatory evidence was misreported and then shut down at trial: "The lab report had erroneously stated that DNA types consistent with Mr. Sutton were found" on a sample that excluded him, and the prosecutor said "I don't want to talk about the unknown sample, okay?"
items.reading: Suppression is quiet containment through documentation, and may be an unintended side effect of routine procedure.
items.loss: This is the specific act of suppression: a prosecutor cutting off exculpatory testimony in open court, not a file being administratively closed.

items.record: His own defence lawyer failed him. The lawyer never authorized the independent testing the family had paid for, retained no expert, and opened the door to questions about a prior conviction: "Well, I'm sorry, man, but that's what they came up with."
items.loss: This is a breakdown by the person who was supposed to be on his side, not a direct clash between him and the institution.

items.record: The same DNA test that implicated him cleared his co-defendant, who "was then released".
items.loss: This is how the flawed evidence sorted two accused people, freeing one and condemning the other.

items.record: The appeals court rejected his ineffective-counsel claim because the DNA evidence "is not seriously challenged".
items.loss: This is the review step that relied on the faulty evidence and so locked in the error.

items.record: His family supported him actively. They paid for testing, and his mother saw the broadcast and "called the station to convince the reporters to investigate her son's case."
items.reading: There is no collective behind the marginal party, who faces the apparatus alone.
items.loss: This is the kin support that actually broke the case open, which the reading denies existed.

items.record: He started post-conviction relief himself, by drafting a motion under a statute that "technically didn't apply to him", and a public defender was then appointed.
items.loss: This is the prisoner acting on his own initiative and using a new legal route that did not formally fit his situation.

items.record: Defence attorneys tipped off TV reporters, who investigated the whole crime lab with independent experts before his case was added: "had begun investigating the Houston crime lab."
items.reading: Press investigation is listed only as one generic possible future source of exposure.
items.loss: This is the outside actors who exposed a lab-wide problem and the order in which that exposure reached his case.

items.record: After he was excluded, prosecutors added conditions, still refused to back innocence, and opposed his habeas petition: "declined to support a pardon based on innocence, noting that the victim had not recanted."
items.loss: This is the institution continuing to resist after it had been proven wrong.

items.record: He was released by a judge and then pardoned by the governor on grounds of innocence, and he received compensation.
items.reading: The file is reopened or exposed, with no specific resolution described.
items.loss: This is the actual outcome, which came through executive clemency and financial redress.

items.record: Years later a database match identified the real attacker, who "pleaded guilty" and named his accomplice.
items.loss: This is the later, independent confirmation of the truth and the identification of the actual offenders.
